title: Sidewalk & delivery robots (PDD laws)
summary: States — not Congress — decide whether autonomous delivery robots can use sidewalks and roads. Over 20 states have passed 'personal delivery device' (PDD) statutes, most granting robots pedestrian-like rights with guardrails. The frontier in 2026 is local pushback: cities weighing surcharges, curfews, and sidewalk-clutter limits.
key_points: More than 20 states authorize sidewalk delivery devices; Pennsylvania’s PDD statute was enacted in 2020 and treats qualifying devices as pedestrians under specified conditions.
Common guardrails: speed caps (often <10 mph), weight limits, yield-to-pedestrian rules, and mandatory liability insurance.
Philadelphia Bill 260526 proposes a $1,000 fee per sidewalk delivery by autonomous units; city records still list it in committee, so it is not an enacted charge.
Liability is unsettled: tort law assumes a human operator, so fault allocation for autonomous devices is being litigated case-by-case.

title: Autonomous vehicles & robotaxis
summary: With no comprehensive federal AV law, states set the rules for testing and deploying self-driving vehicles and robotaxis. The result is a 50-state patchwork: some states authorize driverless deployment by statute, others by executive order, and a few still require a human safety operator.
key_points: Most states have enacted AV legislation or executive orders; a smaller set permit fully driverless commercial deployment.
Robotaxi expansion (Waymo and peers) is governed state-by-state and, in California, by both the DMV and the CPUC.
Key fault lines: state vs. local control, data-sharing/crash-reporting mandates, and insurance minimums.
Sensor and perception suppliers (e.g. 4D imaging radar) ride this demand curve — see the Companies tab.

title: Incentives, R&D credits & site selection
summary: States use broad jobs, investment, and research incentives that robotics firms may qualify for. Program thresholds matter: a large Texas facility and a small Michigan research shop face different eligibility tests.
key_points: Texas Enterprise Fund is a performance-based cash grant, not a robotics tax credit; it requires a competing out-of-state site and significant jobs and investment.
Michigan’s general refundable R&D credit began with 2025 tax years; New York’s Excelsior program lists manufacturing, R&D, and software eligibility with job thresholds.
Pennsylvania’s signed FY2026–27 budget created $125 million Innovate in PA 2.0; California Competes lists three FY2026–27 application windows.
State records and source links appear below on this States page; confirm current application and tax rules with the administering agency.

title: Robotics clusters & workforce pipelines
summary: Several states have built durable robotics ecosystems around anchor universities and non-profit hubs. These clusters shape talent flow, spinouts, and where deployment pilots land first — a structural advantage that incentives alone can't buy.
key_points: Pittsburgh (Carnegie Mellon + Pittsburgh Robotics Network) and Massachusetts (MIT/Harvard + MassRobotics) are the two deepest hubs.
Texas, Michigan (mobility/auto), and California (Bay Area) round out the top tier.
Workforce policy — community-college automation programs, apprenticeships, reskilling grants — is increasingly bundled with incentives.
Cluster strength correlates with spinout density (e.g. CMU → Skild AI; see Companies).

title: State AI laws × autonomous systems & federal preemption
summary: State automated-decision laws can affect some AI uses, but ordinary robot operation is not automatically covered. Colorado changed its law in 2026; its new ADMT Act applies to consequential decisions starting January 1, 2027. The White House March 2026 framework proposes federal preemption in some areas, but Congress has not enacted that proposal.
key_points: Colorado SB 26-189 governs automated technology that materially influences covered consequential decisions; its effective date is January 1, 2027.
The Colorado Attorney General filed draft implementing rules in August 2026; comments and final text remain open.
The March 2026 White House AI framework is legislative advice to Congress, not itself a change in state authority.
For any robot use case, check whether its AI makes a covered decision, then check applicable state and local law.
